oneIdea: MATLAB is built around arrays. Numerical methods turn calculus and algebra into arithmetic on vectors and matrices, so the habit to build is: think in whole arrays, not one number at a time in a loop. Array code is shorter, closer to the maths, and much faster.
goals: Create vectors and matrices with square brackets, zeros, ones and the colon operator.
Read and change elements, rows, columns and blocks with A(rows, cols), : and end.
Tell element-wise operations (.*, .^) from matrix operations (*, ^, \) and use each correctly.
Write a script and a function with if, for and while, and print results with disp and fprintf.
Replace a loop by a vectorized expression or a logical mask such as v(v > 0).

intro.idea: MATLAB means MATrix LABoratory. Its basic data type is the matrix, which is exactly what numerical methods need. The theme of the whole module: think in arrays, not loops.
intro.mistake: Treating MATLAB like a language where every calculation needs a loop over single numbers. Most of the time one array expression does the whole job.

check.q: Why is MATLAB a natural fit for numerical methods?
opts: Because almost everything in numerical methods reduces to operations on vectors and matrices, which are MATLAB's native data type
Because it only works with integers
check.why: Matrices are MATLAB's native type, and numerical methods are mostly vector and matrix operations. MATLAB does have loops, and it handles decimals too.

env.idea: Four panels matter: Command Window (type and see results), Workspace (variables in memory), Editor (your .m files) and Current Folder. A semicolon hides the echo; disp and fprintf print on purpose.
env.mistake: Forgetting the semicolon in finished code, so every line prints its result, or forgetting that clear wipes all your variables from the workspace.

check.why: %.2f means a decimal number with 2 digits after the point, so 3.14159 becomes 3.14. \n starts a new line.

arrays.idea: Everything is an array: a scalar is \(1\times 1\), a row vector \(1\times n\), a column vector \(n\times 1\), a matrix \(m\times n\). Spaces separate columns, semicolons separate rows, and start:step:stop builds evenly spaced vectors.
arrays.mistake: Mixing up spaces and semicolons: [1 2 3] is a row, [1; 2; 3] is a column. They are different shapes.

check.why: The format is start:step:stop. Starting at 10 with step -2 and stopping at 2 gives 10 8 6 4 2.

ops.idea: A(row, col) picks elements; : means all and end means last. A dot before *, / or ^ means element by element; without the dot you get true matrix algebra. To solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) write A\b.
ops.mistake: Forgetting the dot. With x = [2 4 6], x^2 and x*x give an error because a \(1\times3\) vector is not a square matrix; you wanted x.^2 or x.*x.

check.why: The dot means element by element: 2*1, 4*2, 6*3 gives [2 8 18]. The single number 28 would be a dot product, and plain x*y is the one that errors.

prog.idea: A script is a list of commands sharing the workspace. A function has inputs and outputs and its own private workspace, so it is the right tool for any reusable computation. if chooses, for repeats a fixed number of times, while repeats until its condition fails.
prog.mistake: Expecting a function to see the variables of your script. A function has its own private workspace and only knows what you pass in as inputs.

check.q: Which statement about a loop is correct?
opts: for i = 1:5 runs the body 5 times, with i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
check.why: The range 1:5 contains 5 values (both ends included), so the body runs 5 times. A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is true.

vec.idea: Vectorization means working on whole arrays at once instead of looping. It is faster and reads like the maths. A condition like v > 0 creates a logical mask (true/false for every element), and v(mask) picks the marked elements.
vec.mistake: Thinking A(A>15) on a matrix returns a matrix. Reading with a mask returns a column vector (in column-major order). Writing with a mask, such as A(A>15) = 15, keeps the matrix shape.

check.why: v > 0 is the mask [0 0 0 1 1 0 1], and v(mask) keeps the values where it is true: 2, 5, 8. The positions 4 5 7 would come from find(v > 0).

slicing.idea: A(rows, cols) with a range in each position cuts out a block, for example A(2:3, 2:4). Put the slice on the left of = to overwrite it, or assign [] to delete whole rows or columns.
slicing.mistake: Assigning a block of the wrong size. If A(2:3, 2:4) is \(2\times3\), the right-hand side must be \(2\times3\) or a single number. Also, = [] deletes only whole rows or whole columns, never a block in the middle.

check.q: A is \(5\times5\). After A(2, :) = [];, what size is A?
check.why: Assigning [] deletes the 2nd row, so A has 4 rows and still 5 columns. The rows below shift up.
